name: Prometheus Steals Fire
summary: Prometheus, a Titan, stole fire from Mount Olympus and gave it to humanity, enabling civilization. Zeus punished him by chaining him to a rock where an eagle ate his liver daily, only for it to regenerate each night. Heracles eventually freed him. The myth symbolizes the price of knowledge and defiance of divine authority.
significance: Foundational myth about human progress, sacrifice for knowledge, and the tension between divine and human power.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: The Odyssey
summary: After the Trojan War, Odysseus spent ten years trying to return home to Ithaca. He faced the Cyclops, Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the enchantress Circe. Meanwhile, his wife Penelope fended off suitors. The epic explores nostos (homecoming), cunning over brute force, and the costs of hubris.
significance: One of Western literature's foundational texts, establishing the archetype of the hero's journey home.

dna.moralLesson: Cunning can challenge power, but deceit always leaves moral consequences.

dna.moralLesson: Order is never final; every generation must defend meaning against returning chaos.

name: Twelve Labors of Heracles
summary: Driven mad by Hera, Heracles killed his family. As penance, he completed twelve impossible labors: slaying the Nemean Lion, killing the Lernaean Hydra, capturing the Ceryneian Hind, and more. The final labor required him to bring Cerberus from the underworld. These trials earned him immortality.
significance: The archetypal hero's journey of redemption through impossible tasks, copied across countless cultures and stories.

dna.moralLesson: Endurance and sacrifice transform the self and restore balance to the wider community.

summary: Hades abducted Persephone to the underworld. Her mother Demeter, goddess of harvest, caused the earth to become barren in grief. Zeus brokered a compromise: Persephone would spend part of the year below and part above. Her return brings spring; her descent brings winter.
significance: One of the earliest etiological myths explaining seasonal change, central to the Eleusinian Mysteries.

dna.moralLesson: Human flourishing requires aligning personal desire with communal and cosmic responsibility.

summary: Twin sons of Mars and the Vestal Virgin Rhea Silvia, abandoned on the Tiber and raised by a she-wolf. As adults they founded a city, but quarreled over its location. Romulus killed Remus and named the city Rome. The fratricide shadowed Roman history with themes of necessary violence.
significance: Foundation myth that defined Roman identity and justified the city's martial character and territorial expansion.

dna.moralLesson: Human flourishing requires aligning personal desire with communal and cosmic responsibility.

summary: Ragnarök is the prophesied end of the Norse cosmos. Loki breaks free, the Midgard Serpent rises from the sea, Fenrir devours Odin, and Thor and the serpent kill each other. The world sinks into the sea, only to rise again green and renewed. Two human survivors repopulate the earth.
significance: A uniquely Norse concept of cyclical destruction and renewal, where even gods face death — profoundly influencing modern fantasy.

dna.moralLesson: Order is never final; every generation must defend meaning against returning chaos.

name: Epic of Gilgamesh
summary: King Gilgamesh of Uruk, two-thirds god, befriended the wild man Enkidu. Together they slew Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven. When Enkidu died, Gilgamesh sought immortality from flood-survivor Utnapishtim. He found the plant of youth but a serpent stole it. He returned home accepting mortality, his legacy being the walls of Uruk.
significance: The oldest known literary work in human history, establishing themes of friendship, mortality, and the meaning of civilization.

dna.moralLesson: When moral order collapses, survival depends on humility, responsibility, and renewal.

summary: In the Dreamtime, the Rainbow Serpent slithered across the flat land, creating rivers, valleys, and ridges with its massive body. It established the laws of behavior and consequence. Those who obey prosper; those who break the law are turned to stone. It still sleeps in waterways, maintaining the natural order.
significance: One of the world's oldest continuous religious narratives, central to Aboriginal Australian spirituality and land stewardship.

dna.moralLesson: Order is never final; every generation must defend meaning against returning chaos.

summary: Olodumare sent Obatala to create land by pouring sand from a snail shell onto the primordial ocean. A chicken scratched the sand to spread it, forming land. Obatala shaped humans from clay but got drunk on palm wine, creating those with disabilities. Oduduwa completed the task, founding Ile-Ife, the sacred city.
significance: Foundation myth of Yoruba civilization and the city of Ile-Ife, one of the most influential African creation narratives.

dna.moralLesson: Order is never final; every generation must defend meaning against returning chaos.

summary: The eternal sage Väinämöinen commissioned the smith Ilmarinen to forge the Sampo, a magical artifact that produced flour, salt, and gold. It was given to Louhi, mistress of Pohjola (the North), as a bride-price. When Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Lemminkäinen attempted to steal it back, the Sampo was shattered in a sea battle.
significance: Central narrative of Finland's national epic, directly inspiring Tolkien's Silmarillion and the concept of magical artifacts.

dna.moralLesson: Love is powerful, yet trust and restraint decide whether it heals or destroys.

summary: In many Native American traditions, Coyote stole fire from the Fire Spirits to give to humanity. Through cunning and relay races with other animals, the fire was passed until it reached humanity. Coyote's cleverness is balanced by his foolishness. He is both creator and destroyer, teacher and troublemaker.
significance: Coyote is the most widespread trickster figure in Native American mythology, embodying paradox and creative disruption.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

His battle frenzy (ríastrad) transformed him into a terrifying creature.
significance: The central hero of the Ulster Cycle, embodying Celtic warrior ideals and the tragic price of supernatural gifts.

dna.moralLesson: Endurance and sacrifice transform the self and restore balance to the wider community.

summary: Amirani, son of a goddess, stole fire from the heavens and gave it to humanity. As punishment, he was chained to a rock in the Caucasus Mountains where an eagle eternally pecks at his heart. significance: A Caucasian fire-theft myth that may share a common origin with the Greek Prometheus story, predating Indo-European migration.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

significance: Provides the direct Near Eastern source for Hesiod's Theogony, proving mythological transmission across cultures in the ancient world.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

summary: The Nubians believed Jebel Barkal was the primordial mound of creation where the god Amun dwelt inside the mountain. summary: In Georgian tradition, King Aeetes of Colchis guarded the Golden Fleece — the skin of a divine ram that had rescued children from sacrifice. The fleece hung in a sacred grove guarded by a dragon. When Jason came with the Argonauts, Aeetes' daughter Medea betrayed her father out of love. The story reflects Colchis's historical gold wealth.
significance: Georgia (ancient Colchis) was famed for gold-panning using sheepskins, possibly the real origin of the Golden Fleece legend.

dna.moralLesson: Endurance and sacrifice transform the self and restore balance to the wider community.

name: Metamorphoses — Tales of Transformation
summary: Ovid's Metamorphoses weaves 250 transformation myths into a continuous narrative from creation to Julius Caesar's apotheosis. Narcissus becomes a flower, Daphne a laurel tree, Arachne a spider, and Icarus falls from the sky. Each transformation reveals the consequences of hubris, desire, or divine whim.
significance: The single most influential mythological text in Western art, providing source material for Renaissance painting, Shakespeare, and countless later works.

significance: Roman version of the declining-ages concept found across Indo-European mythologies, influencing Western concepts of a lost paradise.

significance: Korea's most famous love story, performed as pansori (narrative singing), representing resistance against corruption and class barriers.

summary: While plowing a field near Tarquinia, a farmer's plow uncovered a child with the wisdom of an elder. This was Tages, a divine being who taught the Etruscans the art of haruspicy (reading entrails), the interpretation of lightning, and the sacred laws (Etrusca disciplina). He then vanished.
significance: Origin myth of Etruscan divination practices that later became central to Roman state religion.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

significance: Foundation myth explaining the origin of evil and suffering, and humanity's enduring capacity for hope.

name: Durga Slays Mahishasura
summary: The buffalo demon Mahishasura received a boon that he could be killed by no god or man. He conquered the heavens. The gods combined their energies to create Durga, a goddess of supreme power. Each god gave her a weapon. After a nine-day battle, she slew Mahishasura, proving that divine feminine power surpasses all.
significance: Central narrative of Durga Puja (Navaratri), one of India's largest festivals, celebrating divine feminine triumph over evil.

dna.moralLesson: Order is never final; every generation must defend meaning against returning chaos.

name: Hou Yi Shoots Down Nine Suns
summary: Ten sun-birds, sons of the sky god Di Jun, decided to cross the sky together, scorching the earth. The divine archer Hou Yi was sent to discipline them. When they refused to return, Hou Yi shot down nine suns, leaving one to light the world. Di Jun was furious and banished Hou Yi from heaven.
significance: Explains why there is only one sun and establishes Hou Yi as a tragic hero — punished for saving humanity, setting up the Chang'e moon myth.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: Changsega — Korean Creation Epic
summary: In the beginning, the giant Mireuk separated heaven and earth and placed four bronze pillars at the corners. He created the sun, moon, and stars from hanging lamps. A rival, Seokga, challenged him to a flower-growing contest. Seokga cheated, but won power over the human world, explaining why evil exists.
significance: A uniquely Korean creation narrative explaining the origin of moral imperfection through a divine contest won through deception.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: Fionn and the Salmon of Knowledge
summary: The druid Finnegas spent seven years fishing for the Salmon of Knowledge in the River Boyne. Young Fionn was tasked with cooking it but burned his thumb on the fish and instinctively sucked it. That taste gave him all the salmon's wisdom. Whenever he needed answers, he sucked his thumb to access infinite knowledge.
significance: Irish origin story for wisdom obtained through accident rather than design — a common Celtic motif where fate overrides intention.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: Ogun Clears the Path to Earth
summary: When the orishas descended from heaven to populate earth, the path was blocked by impenetrable forest. Only Ogun, god of iron, possessed the tools to cut through. He forged a machete and cleared the road. For this service, all orishas honored him. He became patron of blacksmiths, warriors, and all who use metal.
significance: Ogun is one of the most widely worshipped orishas across Africa and the diaspora, patron of technology, roads, and modern progress.

dna.moralLesson: Human flourishing requires aligning personal desire with communal and cosmic responsibility.

name: The Seven Sisters (Pleiades)
summary: Across Aboriginal Australia, the Pleiades are seven sisters fleeing a persistent hunter (Orion). They travel across the land, creating landmarks as they go. When he gets too close, they fly into the sky to escape. The hunter follows, forever chasing them across the heavens. The story maps onto real geography and star movements.
significance: This astronomically grounded narrative spans the entire Australian continent in variations, demonstrating sophisticated stellar observation over tens of thousands of years.

dna.moralLesson: When moral order collapses, survival depends on humility, responsibility, and renewal.

name: Epic of King Gesar
summary: King Gesar was sent from heaven to combat the demons infecting the human world. He was born miraculously, endured exile, and united the fractured tribes of Ling. Through martial prowess and divine wisdom, he defeated demon kings in all four directions. The longest epic in world literature — over a million verses in some versions.
significance: The world's longest epic poem, still performed by living bards across Tibet and Mongolia, representing an unbroken oral tradition spanning centuries.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: Antigone's Defiance
summary: Antigone defied King Creon's edict by burying her brother Polynices, choosing divine law over human law. Creon sentenced her to death. She hanged herself, Creon's son Haemon killed himself at her tomb, and Creon's wife followed. Creon was left destroyed, learning too late that justice cannot be separated from mercy.
significance: Sophocles' exploration of individual conscience versus state authority remains foundational to Western political and ethical thought.

dna.moralLesson: Love is powerful, yet trust and restraint decide whether it heals or destroys.

name: Valhalla — Hall of the Slain
summary: Warriors who died bravely in battle were chosen by the Valkyries to feast in Odin's great hall Valhalla. Each day they fought to the death, each evening they were resurrected to feast on the boar Sæhrímnir and drink mead from the goat Heiðrún. They prepared for the final battle of Ragnarök.
significance: The Norse warrior afterlife ideal profoundly shaped Viking culture, making death in battle the highest honor and fueling the Viking Age expansion.

dna.moralLesson: Order is never final; every generation must defend meaning against returning chaos.

name: Ra's Nightly Journey Through the Duat
summary: Each night, Ra sailed his barque through the twelve hours of the Duat (underworld). In the seventh hour, the chaos serpent Apophis attacked, threatening to swallow the sun forever. Set defended Ra, spearing the serpent. At dawn, Ra emerged reborn as Khepri, the scarab, ensuring another day for the living.
significance: Daily cosmic drama explaining the sun's journey, establishing Set's complex role as both villain (against Osiris) and protector (of Ra).

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: Adapa and Immortality Lost
summary: Adapa, a wise priest of Enki, broke the wing of the South Wind. Summoned before Anu in heaven, Enki warned him not to eat or drink anything offered. Anu, impressed by Adapa's wisdom, offered the food and water of immortality. Following Enki's advice, Adapa refused — and humanity lost its chance at eternal life.
significance: One of the earliest narratives about humanity's loss of immortality through trickery or error, predating similar biblical themes by centuries.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: The Four Ayar Brothers
summary: Four brothers and four sisters emerged from caves at Pacaritambo. The strongest brother, Ayar Cachi, was sealed in a cave by his jealous siblings because his sling could crumble mountains. One brother turned to stone as a boundary marker. Ayar Manco (Manco Capac) and Mama Ocllo finally founded Cusco.
significance: The sibling-rivalry foundation myth of Cusco and the Inca dynasty, linking royal authority to emergence from the earth itself.

summary: The monkey god Hanuman, son of Vayu (Wind), volunteered to leap across the ocean to Lanka to find the captured Sita. He overcame Surasa, a sea demoness, and Simhika who tried to catch his shadow. He found Sita, delivered Rama's ring, set Lanka ablaze with his burning tail, and returned triumphant.
significance: Hanuman's devotion to Rama is the supreme example of bhakti (devotion) in Hinduism — he is worshipped across South and Southeast Asia.

dna.moralLesson: Love is powerful, yet trust and restraint decide whether it heals or destroys.

summary: Nezha was born from a flesh ball after three years' pregnancy. As a child, he killed the Dragon King's son while bathing in the sea, causing cosmic outrage. To save his parents from divine punishment, he carved his own flesh from his bones and returned it to them. His master resurrected him with lotus flowers.
significance: Nezha represents filial rebellion and self-sacrifice, embodying the Chinese cultural tension between obedience and individual justice.

dna.moralLesson: Endurance and sacrifice transform the self and restore balance to the wider community.

name: Crow and the Seven Emu Women
summary: Crow was clever but hungry. He discovered the Emu Women had fire but wouldn't share. He prepared a fake wound full of ants and pretended to be injured. When the women came to help, he tricked them into gathering sticks. He stole their hidden firestick and flew away, but dropped embers across creation, giving fire to all.
significance: Aboriginal fire-origin tale explaining how fire spread across the landscape, connecting ecological knowledge with moral narrative.

dna.moralLesson: Knowledge can elevate humanity, but it always carries ethical responsibility and cost.

name: Noah and the Great Flood
summary: Human corruption leads to divine judgment through a world-flood. Noah receives warning, builds an ark, preserves life, and emerges into a renewed covenantal order.
significance: A foundational flood narrative in Biblical tradition and a major comparative node for Ancient Near Eastern transmission debates.

dna.moralLesson: Moral accountability and disciplined preparation can preserve life during civilizational collapse.
